claims.text: High configurational entropy causes sluggish atomic diffusion in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Sluggish atomic diffusion governs the high-temperature structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys.
Sluggish atomic diffusion inhibits phase segregation in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Sluggish atomic diffusion inhibits grain growth in high-entropy nanoalloys.
The initial high-entropy nanoparticles have a uniform distribution of multiple principal elements.
The controlled comparison uses a high-entropy nanoalloy with at least five principal elements and a low-entropy alloy with fewer principal elements.
The high-entropy and low-entropy samples will be processed identically.
The samples will receive the same thermal exposure, atmosphere, and duration.
Particle size will be controlled between the samples.
High configurational entropy reduces atomic mobility and diffusion rates in the alloy.
The presence of multiple elements creates a complex energy landscape.
The complex energy landscape raises local energy barriers for atomic migration.
Higher local migration barriers slow diffusion.
Slower diffusion mitigates phase segregation and grain coarsening at high temperature.
After high-temperature treatment, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit less grain coarsening than the low-entropy control.
After high-temperature treatment, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit less phase segregation than the low-entropy control.
The prediction is limited to compositional ranges, particle sizes, and temperature regimes typical of high-entropy nanoalloy applications.
Substantial changes in atmosphere or thermal-exposure time may alter the predicted behavior.
Protective oxide formation may contribute to observed high-temperature stability.
Intermetallic-compound formation may contribute to observed high-temperature stability.
